content: A dental impression is a precise and detailed replica of a portion or the entirety of a patient’s dentition, as well as other structures within the oral cavity. It serves as a negative mold of the teeth and gums, which can subsequently be utilized to create a physical cast or model of the dentition. This model is essential for the construction of dental prostheses such as dentures, crowns, or other restorative devices. The process of taking a dental impression involves introducing a viscous liquid material into the patient’s mouth, typically using a tray that is customized to fit the individual’s oral anatomy. Once placed, the material undergoes a setting process, transforming into an elastic solid. Upon removal from the mouth, the material retains an accurate imprint of the teeth and surrounding structures. Commonly employed materials for dental impressions include sodium alginate, polyether, and silicones. Silicones are further categorized into condensation-cured silicones and addition-cured silicones, the latter often referred to as polyvinyl siloxane. Historically, other materials such as plaster of Paris, zinc oxide-eugenol, and agar were also used for this purpose.
